Regression part 2

Goals for this section

  • Prior choice
  • Fit indices
  • Robust regression
  • Handle categorical variables
  • ANOVA and Post-hoc tests

Everything plotted against everything

Code 
library(GGally)
ggpairs(week3)

Model

\[\text{Health}_i \sim \text{Normal}(\mu_i, \sigma)\] \[\mu_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 (\text{Happy}_i - \overline{\text{Happy}})\]

\[\beta_0 \sim \text{Normal}(0, 5) \qquad \beta_1 \sim \text{Normal}(0, 5)\] \[\sigma \sim \text{HalfCauchy}(0, 10)\]

What do these priors mean? How did we come up with them?

Visualizing the priors

Code 
library(brms)
library(tidybayes)

prior.1 <- prior(normal(0, 5), class = Intercept) +
                prior(normal(0, 5), class = b) +
                prior(cauchy(0, 10), class = sigma)

prior.1 %>% 
  parse_dist(prior) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(y=class, dist =.dist, args=.args)) +
  stat_halfeye()+
  scale_x_continuous( limits = c(-50, 50))+
  labs(title="Priors")

Prior Predictive Distribution

AKA what does our model think is possible before we give it any data

Code 
library(brms)

week3 <- week3 %>% 
  mutate(happy_c = happy - mean(happy))

h.1p <- 
  brm(family = gaussian,
      health ~ 1 + happy_c,
      prior = prior.1,
      data = week3,
      sample_prior = "only",
      iter = 1000, warmup = 500, chains = 2, cores = 2, 
      backend = "cmdstanr",
      file = "h.1p")

Prior Predictive gives impossible values

pp_check(h.1p) + xlim(-35,35)

This graphs 10 simulated datasets from the prior predictive distribution, compared to our actual data’s density

Prior predictive: intervals by person

pp_check(h.1p,
         type = 'intervals')

The slopes are too large

Code 
library(modelr)

week3 %>% 
data_grid(happy_c = seq_range(happy_c, n = 101)) %>% 
 add_epred_draws(h.1p, ndraws = 100) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = happy_c, y = health)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = .epred, group = .draw), alpha = .1) +
  xlab("happy (centered)")

What if we try strange priors?

What happens if we try strange priors?

Code 
prior.2 <- prior(normal(-5, 2), class = Intercept) +
                prior(normal(10, 5), class = b) +
                prior(cauchy(3, 1), class = sigma)
h.1p2 <- 
  brm(family = gaussian,
      health ~ 1 + happy_c,
      prior = prior.2,
      data = week3,
      sample_prior = "only",
      iter = 1000, warmup = 500, chains = 2, cores = 2, 
      backend = "cmdstanr",
      file = "h.1p2")

The strange priors

Code 
prior.2 %>% 
  parse_dist(prior) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(y=class, dist =.dist, args=.args)) +
  stat_halfeye()+
  scale_x_continuous( limits = c(-25, 25)) +
  labs(title="strange priors")

Does this make sense?

Code 
week3 %>% 
data_grid(happy_c = seq_range(happy_c, n = 101)) %>% 
 add_epred_draws(h.1p2, ndraws = 100) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = happy_c, y = health)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = .epred, group = .draw), alpha = .1) +
  xlab("happy (centered)")

Fit model

We just saw that Normal(0, 5) priors allow impossible health values. We’ll fit with them anyway, on purpose: with 200 people the data swamp them (compare the strange-prior fit a few slides from now). With smaller samples or more complex models, you would tighten them.

Code 
h.1 <- 
  brm(family = gaussian,
      health ~ 1 + happy_c,
      prior = c(prior(normal(0, 5), class = Intercept),
                prior(normal(0, 5), class = b),
                prior(cauchy(0, 10), class = sigma)),
      data = week3,
      iter = 1000, warmup = 500, chains = 2, cores = 2, 
      backend = "cmdstanr",
      file = "h.1")

Results with our priors (99% intervals)

summary(h.1, prob = .99)
 Family: gaussian 
  Links: mu = identity 
Formula: health ~ 1 + happy_c 
   Data: week3 (Number of observations: 200) 
  Draws: 2 chains, each with iter = 1000; warmup = 500; thin = 1;
         total post-warmup draws = 1000

Regression Coefficients:
          Estimate Est.Error l-99% CI u-99% CI Rhat Bulk_ESS Tail_ESS
Intercept     8.50      0.20     8.03     9.03 1.00     1056      722
happy_c       0.34      0.13    -0.02     0.66 1.00      968      641

Further Distributional Parameters:
      Estimate Est.Error l-99% CI u-99% CI Rhat Bulk_ESS Tail_ESS
sigma     2.81      0.15     2.44     3.22 1.01      737      612

Draws were sampled using sample(hmc). For each parameter, Bulk_ESS
and Tail_ESS are effective sample size measures, and Rhat is the potential
scale reduction factor on split chains (at convergence, Rhat = 1).

What did the strange priors move?

Code 
library(patchwork)
both <- bind_rows("Normal(0, 5) priors" = spread_draws(h.1, b_Intercept, b_happy_c),
                  "strange priors"      = spread_draws(h.1b, b_Intercept, b_happy_c), .id = "priors")
p.int   <- ggplot(both, aes(x = b_Intercept, fill = priors)) + stat_slab(alpha = .6) +
  labs(x = "intercept (health at average happiness)", y = NULL)
p.slope <- ggplot(both, aes(x = b_happy_c, fill = priors)) + stat_slab(alpha = .6) +
  labs(x = "slope (health per unit of happiness)", y = NULL)
(p.int | p.slope) + plot_layout(guides = "collect") &
  theme_classic(base_size = 14) & theme(legend.position = "bottom") & scale_y_continuous(breaks = NULL)
  • Slope: barely moved. Its strange prior, Normal(10, 5), is wide compared with what the data say (posterior SD ≈ 0.13)
  • Intercept: moved from 8.50 to 8.37. Normal(−5, 2) is much tighter. Roughly, the posterior is a precision-weighted average: data precision 1/0.2² = 25 vs. prior 1/2² = 0.25, so the prior gets ~1% of the weight: 1% × (8.5 − (−5)) ≈ 0.13

priors

  • With enough data, priors do not really matter
  • With simple models, we can envision what priors make sense. With more complex, prior predictives will be very helpful
  • Unless you have previous studies or population-level statistics, use weakly informative priors: slopes centered on 0, intercepts on a plausible value of the outcome (lecture 2). These rule out absurd values without overly influencing results

Today’s posterior is tomorrow’s prior, in brms

Lecture 1 did this exactly on a grid. In brms, the posterior is draws, not a formula, so we summarize it as normal priors:

Code 
set.seed(27)
half <- sample(nrow(week3), nrow(week3) / 2)
h.s1 <- update(h.1, newdata = week3[half, ], seed = 27, file = "h.s1")        # wave 1

p1 <- fixef(h.s1)                                                           # wave 1 posterior → wave 2 prior
prior.seq <- c(prior_string(sprintf("normal(%.3f, %.3f)", p1["Intercept", "Estimate"], p1["Intercept", "Est.Error"]), class = "Intercept"),
               prior_string(sprintf("normal(%.3f, %.3f)", p1["happy_c", "Estimate"],   p1["happy_c", "Est.Error"]),   class = "b"),
               prior(cauchy(0, 10), class = sigma))
h.s2 <- update(h.1, newdata = week3[-half, ], prior = prior.seq, seed = 27, file = "h.s2")   # wave 2
prior.seq
                prior     class coef group resp dpar nlpar   lb   ub tag source
 normal(8.641, 0.306) Intercept                            <NA> <NA>       user
 normal(0.257, 0.200)         b                            <NA> <NA>       user
        cauchy(0, 10)     sigma                            <NA> <NA>       user

Two steps vs. all at once

Code 
bind_rows("wave 1 alone"                   = as_tibble(fixef(h.s1), rownames = "par"),
          "wave 2, wave 1's posterior as prior" = as_tibble(fixef(h.s2), rownames = "par"),
          "all 200 at once"                = as_tibble(fixef(h.1), rownames = "par"), .id = "fit") %>%
  filter(par == "happy_c") %>% select(-par) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 2)))
# A tibble: 3 × 5
  fit                                 Estimate Est.Error  Q2.5 Q97.5
  <chr>                                  <dbl>     <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1 wave 1 alone                            0.26      0.2  -0.13  0.63
2 wave 2, wave 1's posterior as prior     0.36      0.14  0.09  0.63
3 all 200 at once                         0.34      0.13  0.07  0.58

Close, but only approximately. Summarizing wave 1 by a mean and an SD per parameter throws away:

  • the posterior’s shape (fine here: it’s nearly normal)
  • the correlation between intercept and slope (small here, thanks to centering)
  • everything about σ, which started over from its original prior

The grid in lecture 1 carried the whole posterior forward, so it was exact. (This is HW 3 Q2c.)

Wide or long draws (recap)

Same draws, two shapes: spread_draws() gives one column per parameter (handy for computing), gather_draws() one row per parameter per draw (handy for plotting and summarizing several at once).

h.1 %>% spread_draws(b_Intercept, b_happy_c, sigma) %>% head(3)
# A tibble: 3 × 6
  .chain .iteration .draw b_Intercept b_happy_c sigma
   <int>      <int> <int>       <dbl>     <dbl> <dbl>
1      1          1     1        8.44     0.257  3.21
2      1          2     2        8.40     0.273  3.13
3      1          3     3        8.20     0.567  3.09
h.1 %>% gather_draws(b_Intercept, b_happy_c, sigma) %>% mean_qi()
# A tibble: 3 × 7
  .variable   .value .lower .upper .width .point .interval

model fit

  • So far the model is the same as frequentist. The major difference is in the posterior, but even then we can use what we know about sampling to get estimates, fitted values, CIs, etc.

  • How can we evaluate our model like we normally do? R2 is most common, however, we will have additional tricks up our sleeve (eg waic, loo – similar to AIC/BIC, likelihood ratio tests etc).

One R² per draw

Every draw is a different set of regression coefficients, and every set of coefficients has its own R².

Code 
head(bayes_R2(h.1, summary = F)) # summary = FALSE gives one R2 per draw
              R2
[1,] 0.018774365
[2,] 0.021114391
[3,] 0.084035312
[4,] 0.099795697
[5,] 0.004291684
[6,] 0.014306886

Typically R2 is the variance of the predicted values divided by total variance. But for Bayes we have 1) many predicted values (1 for each sample) and 2) we want to incorporate uncertainty in the estimates

Bayesian R2

This is a summary of our 1000 R2 values. Like other parameters it has a distribution.

Code 
bayes_R2(h.1, summary = T) # summary = TRUE gives a summary
     Estimate  Est.Error        Q2.5      Q97.5
R2 0.03555034 0.02269733 0.001622928 0.08806008

Bayesian R², precisely

For each posterior draw s, brms computes

\[R^2_s = \frac{\text{Var}(\hat{y}^{(s)})}{\text{Var}(\hat{y}^{(s)}) + \text{Var}(e^{(s)})}\]

  • \(\hat{y}^{(s)}\): the expected values (epred) for every person under draw s; \(e^{(s)} = y - \hat{y}^{(s)}\): the residuals under that draw
  • Explained variance over explained + residual variance, like the usual R², but computed once per draw, so R² gets its own posterior distribution (and interval)
  • Plugging posterior draws into the classical \(\text{Var}(\hat{y}) / \text{Var}(y)\) can give values above 1 (e.g., with strong priors); this version can’t, and it reflects our uncertainty about the coefficients (Gelman, Goodrich, Gabry & Vehtari, 2019)

Categorical Variable coding

Of course anytime we use group variables we need to assign them numeric values. How does that work in Bayesian land? Mostly the same but

  1. We need to be careful about our priors

  2. We will manipulate the posterior to get what we want

  3. There is an additional coding option that is often helpful

Categorical data

Code 
library(forcats)
week3 <-week3 %>% 
  mutate(mood.group.d = mood.group %>%
           factor() %>% 
           fct_recode("control" = "0", "tx" ="1","tx" = "2")) 
       
table(week3$mood.group.d)

     66     134

mood.group has three groups (0 = control, 1 and 2 = two treatment arms). To keep the first example to two groups, we combine the treatment arms; the ANOVA section at the end has a three-group example.

Index variables

  • There are two priors for the group coded 1. One prior on the difference and one on the intercept.

  • What we could do instead is not fit an intercept and instead directly model two group means.

  • While possible in a frequentist framework it is a little awkward because it is not easy to test the hypothesis that the groups differ

  • If you have 20 groups, that is a lot of priors (one for each dummy!), but with this approach there is a single prior for all levels/factors

Index-coded model

h.3 <- 
  brm(family = gaussian,
      health ~ 0 + mood.group.d,
      prior = c(prior(normal(0, 10), class = b),
                prior(cauchy(0, 10), class = sigma)),
      data = week3,
      iter = 1000, warmup = 500, chains = 2, cores = 2, 
      backend = "cmdstanr",
      file = "h.3")

We suppress the intercept by putting in a 0. This “no intercept” model is a general strategy for working with categorical data within Bayes.

Why lm’s R² breaks without an intercept

Note the ridiculous R². Without an intercept, lm() measures R² against 0 instead of the mean of y, so the group means themselves count as “explained.” The F test changes too (it now tests whether the means are 0).

test2 <- lm(health ~ 0 + mood.group.d, data = week3)
summary(test2)

Same posterior, different parameterization

  • All info you need is in the posterior.
  • It is the same posterior distribution as before
Code 
h.3 %>%
  gather_draws(b_mood.group.dcontrol, b_mood.group.dtx) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x= .value, y = .variable)) +
  stat_halfeye()

Index variables: fewer priors

  • In addition to getting everything you want from a categorical variables, an additional benefit is fewer priors!

  • Think about a prior for 4 group/level variable where you have to have a new dummy for each of them. Each dummy would be a new parameter where you have to add a prior. With index coding there is one prior for all groups AND they are on the mean of the category rather than the difference.

Dummy or index coding?

Dummy coding y ~ 1 + group Index coding y ~ 0 + group
Parameters reference-group mean + differences from it one mean per group
Priors reference mean + one per difference (different scales!) one prior on the group-mean scale, for all groups
Group means intercept + difference, per draw read directly
Differences read directly (vs. reference only) subtract per draw (any pair)
Best when differences from one baseline matter, or other predictors group means matter, or many groups

Same model, same group-mean posteriors (with comparable priors): the choice is about priors and readability.

post hoc tests

Two ways we’ll use all semester:

  • “By hand”: compute the difference from the draws (what we did for the dummy-coded model)
  • {marginaleffects}: avg_predictions(..., by = , hypothesis = ), which does the same thing for you

brms’s hypothesis() is handy for one thing below: one-sided questions. ({emmeans} also works with brms models, e.g. emmeans(h.3, "mood.group.d") |> pairs(), but we’ll stick with marginaleffects.)

One-sided hypotheses and Post.Prob

hyp.3 <- hypothesis(h.3, "mood.group.dtx > mood.group.dcontrol")
hyp.3
Hypothesis Tests for class b:
                Hypothesis Estimate Est.Error CI.Lower CI.Upper Evid.Ratio
1 (mood.group.dtx)-... > 0     0.79      0.42     0.11     1.45      33.48
  Post.Prob Star
1      0.97    *
---
'CI': 90%-CI for one-sided and 95%-CI for two-sided hypotheses.
'*': For one-sided hypotheses, the posterior probability exceeds 95%;
for two-sided hypotheses, the value tested against lies outside the 95%-CI.
Posterior probabilities of point hypotheses assume equal prior probabilities.

Post.Prob is the share of posterior draws in which tx > control: the posterior probability that the difference is positive. You can get the same number by hand with mean(diff > 0) on the draws. Unlike a p-value, it’s a probability about the effect, not about the data. (Week 6 calls this the “probability of direction.”)

1      0.83     
---
'CI': 90%-CI for one-sided and 95%-CI for two-sided hypotheses.
'*': For one-sided hypotheses, the posterior probability exceeds 95%;
for two-sided hypotheses, the value tested against lies outside the 95%-CI.
Posterior probabilities of point hypotheses assume equal prior probabilities.

Same idea: Post.Prob is the share of draws in which the tx mean is below 9.

Extending the basic model

Now we have the basics down we can extend the model, tweaking different components of it. We have already seen what happens if we tweak the priors a little. Thus far they have been mostly inconsequential.

What if we tweak the likelihood and model?

  1. Robust regression

  2. Heterogeneous variances

Robust regression

  • How do you treat “outliers”? Why not incorporate our model to expect outliers, especially when working with low N situations?

  • Enter the t-distribution, with its heavy tailed distributions. Alternatively, a “robust” estimation could use medians instead of means

  • (Note that a frequentist t-test does not assume a t DGP – only that the sampling distribution is distributed as a t, just like any linear model).

Robust Model

\[\text{Health}_i \sim t(\nu, \mu_i, \sigma) \qquad \mu_i = \alpha_{\text{Group}[i]}\]

\[\nu \sim \text{Gamma}(1, 0.1) \qquad \alpha_j \sim \text{Normal}(0, 10)\] \[\sigma \sim \text{HalfCauchy}(0, 1)\]

Index coded, like h.3: one mean per group.

gamma prior

Code 
prior(gamma(1, .1), class = nu) %>% 
  parse_dist(prior) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(y=class, dist =.dist, args=.args)) +
  stat_halfeye()+
  labs(title="Prior")

The t distribution at different df

Code 
expand.grid(
  df = c(.5, 1,2,3,5,10,30,50),
  scale = c(1)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(y = 0, dist = "student_t", arg1 = df, arg2 = 0, arg3 = scale, color = ordered(df))) +
  stat_slab(p_limits = c(.01, .99), fill = NA) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = NULL) +
  facet_grid( ~ scale)+ xlim(-6,6)

Robust model

h.4R <- 
  brm(family = student,
      health ~ 0 + mood.group.d,
      prior = c(prior(gamma(1, .1), class = nu),
                prior(normal(0, 10), class = b),
                prior(cauchy(0, 1),  class = sigma)),
      backend = "cmdstanr",
      file = "h.4R",
      data = week3)

Fixing ν

Instead of estimating ν we can fix it low, which guarantees fat tails no matter what the data say. (Estimating ν, as above, lets the data choose skinnier tails.)

  • ν = 3 is a common choice: about 6% of the distribution lies beyond ±3 scale units, vs. 0.3% for a normal, and the SD still exists
  • Smaller ν = fatter tails. ν = 1 is the extreme (it has its own name, the Cauchy distribution). Its tails are so heavy that the model treats much of the data as outliers and acts almost like the median, and the SD no longer exists
h.5R <- 
  brm(family = student,
      bf(health ~ 0 + mood.group.d, nu = 3),
      prior = c(prior(normal(0, 10), class = b),
                prior(cauchy(0, 1),  class = sigma)),
      file = "h.5R3",
      backend = "cmdstanr",
      data = week3)

For a t, σ isn’t the SD

σ dropped from about 2.8 (normal) to 2.3 (ν = 3). The data didn’t change: for a t, σ is a scale, and \(\text{SD} = \sigma \sqrt{\nu / (\nu - 2)}\). That needs ν > 2: with heavier tails the SD is infinite, whatever σ is (one more reason to fix ν at 3, not 1).

Code 
bind_rows(
  "normal (h.3)"          = spread_draws(h.3, sigma) %>% mutate(nu = Inf),
  "t, ν estimated (h.4R)" = spread_draws(h.4R, sigma, nu),
  "t, ν = 3 (h.5R)"       = spread_draws(h.5R, sigma) %>% mutate(nu = 3), .id = "model") %>%
  mutate(SD = sigma * sqrt(ifelse(is.finite(nu), nu / (nu - 2), 1))) %>%
  group_by(model) %>%
  summarise(sigma = median(sigma), nu = median(nu), SD = median(SD)) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 2)))
# A tibble: 3 × 4
  model                 sigma    nu    SD
  <chr>                 <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1 normal (h.3)           2.82 Inf    2.82
2 t, ν = 3 (h.5R)        2.27   3    3.93
3 t, ν estimated (h.4R)  2.7   20.4  2.86
  • Compare SDs, not σs, across likelihoods
  • h.4R estimated ν ≈ 20: these data aren’t very heavy-tailed. Forcing ν = 3 on them makes the implied SD (about 3.9) bigger than the normal model’s. Fix ν when you expect outliers; otherwise estimate it

Robust vs. non-robust, with outliers

Suppose three control participants’ scores were entered wrong (25 instead of 2.5), and we didn’t check for or exclude them. Same two models and priors; only the likelihood differs.

Code 
week3.out <- week3 %>%
  bind_rows(tibble(health = c(25, 25, 25),
                   mood.group.d = factor("control", levels = levels(week3$mood.group.d))))
h.3.out  <- update(h.3,  newdata = week3.out, seed = 27, file = "h.3out")    # normal
h.4R.out <- update(h.4R, newdata = week3.out, seed = 27, file = "h.4Rout")   # t, ν estimated

bind_rows("normal"          = avg_predictions(h.3.out,  by = "mood.group.d") %>% get_draws(),
          "t (ν estimated)" = avg_predictions(h.4R.out, by = "mood.group.d") %>% get_draws(), .id = "model") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = draw, y = mood.group.d, colour = model)) +
  stat_pointinterval(position = position_dodge(width = .4), .width = c(.66, .95)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#0072B2", "#D55E00")) +
  labs(x = "group mean health (66% and 95% intervals)", y = NULL, colour = NULL) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 14) + theme(legend.position = "top")
  • Normal: three bad scores pull the control mean up to 8.72 and inflate σ; the group difference nearly vanishes (0.03; about 0.8 without the bad scores)
  • t: heavy tails let it treat the 25s as rare draws: control 8.18, difference 0.61
  • ν is a diagnostic: estimated ν ≈ 5; a small ν flags outliers worth a look

relaxing equal variance assumption

One assumption that often gets relaxed in ANOVA and other group models is the assumption that there are equal variances. Welch’s t-test does not assume groups to have equal variances.

We could run a model that is both robust and has no equal variance assumption.

Two ways to relax equal variances

Robust and unequal variances

Health ~ T( \(\nu\) , \(\mu_i\) , \(\sigma_i\) )

\(\mu_i\) = \(\beta_0\) + \(\beta_1\) \(Group_i\)
log(\(\sigma_i\)) = \(\gamma_0\) + \(\gamma_1\) \(Group_i\)

\(\nu\) ~ Gamma(2,.1)
\(\beta_0\) ~ Normal(0, 10)
\(\beta_1\) ~ Normal(0, 3)
\(\gamma_0\) ~ Normal(0, 10)
\(\gamma_1\) ~ Normal(0, 3)

Welch’s, but not robust

Health ~ Normal( \(\mu_i\) , \(\sigma_i\) )

\(\mu_i\) = \(\beta_0\) + \(\beta_1\) \(Group_i\)
log(\(\sigma_i\)) = \(\gamma_0\) + \(\gamma_1\) \(Group_i\)

\(\beta_0\) ~ Normal(0, 10)
\(\beta_1\) ~ Normal(0, 10)
\(\gamma_0\) ~ Normal(0, 3)
\(\gamma_1\) ~ Normal(0, 3)

Index version

Index variable for robust and unequal variances

Health ~ T( \(\nu\) , \(\mu_i\) , \(\sigma_i\) )

\(\mu_i\) = \(\alpha_{\text{Group}[i]}\)
log(\(\sigma_i\)) = \(\gamma_{\text{Group}[i]}\)

\(\nu\) ~ Gamma(2,.1)
\(\alpha_j\) ~ Normal(8, 3)
\(\gamma_j\) ~ Normal(0, 3)

Group means of health (which averages about 8.5) get Normal(8, 3). \(\gamma_j\) is log(σ), so Normal(0, 3) is a wide prior there.

Robust, unequal variances: dummy coding

h.6 <- 
  brm(family = student,
     bf( health ~ 1 + mood.group.d,
         sigma ~ 1 + mood.group.d),
      prior = c(prior(gamma(2, .1), class = nu),
                prior(normal(0, 10), class = Intercept),
                prior(normal(0, 3), class = b),
                prior(normal(0, 10), class = Intercept, dpar = sigma),
                prior(normal(0, 3), class = b, dpar = sigma)),
     file = "h.6.rds",
     backend = "cmdstanr",
     data = week3)

Back to the SD scale

The sigmas are modeled through a (natural) log link (to constrain them to be positive). Convert log values (which range from −∞ to ∞) back to the original scale with exp().

Code 
post.h7 <- h.7 %>% 
  spread_draws(b_mood.group.dcontrol,b_mood.group.dtx, b_sigma_mood.group.dcontrol,b_sigma_mood.group.dtx) %>% 
  transmute(`Control`     = b_mood.group.dcontrol,
            `Tx`  = b_mood.group.dtx,
            `Sigma Control`    = b_sigma_mood.group.dcontrol%>% exp(),
            `Sigma Tx` = b_sigma_mood.group.dtx %>% exp()) %>% 
  mutate(`Differences`  = `Tx` - `Control`,
         `Sigma Difference` = `Sigma Tx` - `Sigma Control`,
         `Effect Size` = (`Differences`) / sqrt((`Sigma Control`^2 + `Sigma Tx`^2) / 2))

# A tibble: 1 × 6

1                     0.987  0.783   1.23   0.95 median qi
Code 
mean(post.h7$`Sigma Tx` > post.h7$`Sigma Control`)
[1] 0.45525

The ratio’s interval comfortably includes 1, and the probability that Tx is more variable is near a coin flip: no evidence the groups differ in spread, so the equal-variance model was fine here.

The modeling toolbox: two choices

1. Pick a likelihood that matches your outcome. Today we swapped the Normal for a Student-t to handle outliers. We’ll make the same move again:

Outcome Likelihood When
continuous Normal weeks 2–3
continuous, with outliers Student-t today
0/1 (yes/no) Bernoulli: logistic regression week 7
counts (0, 1, 2, …) Poisson or negative binomial week 8

2. Decide what to do with each of its parameters. The parameters come with the likelihood: a Normal has μ and σ; a t has μ, σ, and ν. For each one, you can:

  • fix it at a value (ν = 3)
  • estimate it as one number (ν, or a single σ)
  • give it an equation, so it changes with predictors (μ by group; σ by group)

Any parameter can get an equation

We’re used to an equation for μ. Nothing is special about μ:

\[\text{Health}_i \sim \text{Normal}(\mu_i, \sigma_i)\] \[\mu_i = \alpha_{\text{Group}[i]} \qquad \log(\sigma_i) = \gamma_{\text{Group}[i]}\]

  • “Do the groups differ in their average?” → a predictor on μ
  • “Do the groups differ in their variability?” → a predictor on σ. Same question, different parameter
  • Parameters with limits get a link so the equation can’t go out of bounds: log for σ (> 0), logit for a probability (0 to 1, logistic regression)

So the recipe for any data situation: choose the likelihood, then decide which of its parameters to fix, estimate, or model. Every later model in the course (logistic, counts, multilevel, distributional) is these two choices again.

ANOVA models

So far we’ve compared two groups, a Bayesian t-test. The same model extends to three or more groups: a Bayesian ANOVA.

The study (simulated, so we know the truth): 120 people are randomly assigned to watch 10 minutes of a statistics lecture, cat videos, or puppy videos, then rate their happiness (0–10).

Code 
set.seed(2027)
videos <- tibble(video = factor(rep(c("lecture", "cats", "puppies"), each = 40),
                                levels = c("lecture", "cats", "puppies")),
                 true_mean = c(lecture = 4.5, cats = 6.0, puppies = 6.4)[as.character(video)],
                 happiness = pmin(pmax(rnorm(120, true_mean, 1.5), 0), 10)) %>%  # keep on the 0–10 scale
  select(-true_mean)

videos %>% group_by(video) %>% summarise(n = n(), mean = mean(happiness), sd = sd(happiness))
# A tibble: 3 × 4
  video       n  mean    sd
  <fct>   <int> <dbl> <dbl>
1 lecture    40  4.76  1.47
2 cats       40  5.91  1.59
3 puppies    40  6.37  1.51

ANOVA More than 2 groups

happiness\(_i\) ~ Normal( \(\mu_i\) , \(\sigma\) )

\(\mu_i\) = \(\alpha_{\text{Video}[i]}\)

\(\alpha_j\) ~ Normal(5, 2) , for j = lecture, cats, puppies
\(\sigma\) ~ Exponential(1)

Fitting the ANOVA model

Note that we have one prior for all our groups

a.1 <- 
  brm(family = gaussian,
      happiness ~ 0 + video,
      prior = c(prior(normal(5, 2), class = b),
                prior(exponential(1), class = sigma)),
      iter = 2000, warmup = 1000, chains = 2, cores = 2,
      data = videos,
      sample_prior = "yes",
      backend = "cmdstanr",
      file = "a.1videos")

The group-mean prior

Code 
prior.a.1 %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = b)) +
  geom_density() +
  labs(x = "a group's mean happiness (prior)") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())

A parameter per group

get_variables(a.1)
 [1] "b_videolecture" "b_videocats"    "b_videopuppies" "sigma"         
 [5] "prior_b"        "prior_sigma"    "lprior"         "lp__"          
 [9] "accept_stat__"  "treedepth__"    "stepsize__"     "divergent__"   
[13] "n_leapfrog__"   "energy__"

Notice that we have a parameter for each group mean

Group-mean posteriors

Code 
a.1 %>% 
  gather_draws(b_videolecture, b_videocats, b_videopuppies) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(y = .variable, x = .value)) +
  stat_halfeye() +
  labs(x = "mean happiness", y = NULL)

Post hoc tests

Our posterior captures all information in the model. Thus any sort of additional information we may want (eg group comparison) we can get through manipulating our posterior!

post.a.1 <- a.1 %>% 
  spread_draws(b_videolecture, b_videocats, b_videopuppies, sigma) %>% 
  mutate(`cats − lecture`    = b_videocats    - b_videolecture,
         `puppies − lecture` = b_videopuppies - b_videolecture,
         `puppies − cats`    = b_videopuppies - b_videocats,
         `d: cats − lecture`    = `cats − lecture` / sigma,
         `d: puppies − lecture` = `puppies − lecture` / sigma,
         `d: puppies − cats`    = `puppies − cats` / sigma)

The differences, draw by draw

post.a.1 %>% select(.draw, `cats − lecture`:`puppies − cats`)
# A tibble: 2,000 × 4
   .draw `cats − lecture` `puppies − lecture` `puppies − cats`
   <int>            <dbl>               <dbl>            <dbl>
 1     1            0.818                1.19            0.369
 2     2            0.687                1.08            0.395
 3     3            1.05                 2.13            1.08 
 4     4            0.761                1.30            0.538
 5     5            1.06                 1.78            0.721
 6     6            1.11                 1.78            0.672
 7     7            0.931                1.65            0.719
 8     8            0.942                1.61            0.666

10    10            1.59                 1.69            0.103

Plotting the differences

Code 
post.a.1 %>% 
  gather_draws(`cats − lecture`, `puppies − lecture`, `puppies − cats`) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(y = .variable, x = .value)) +
  stat_halfeye() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = 2) +
  labs(x = "difference in mean happiness", y = NULL)

Summarizing the differences

post.a.1 %>% 
  gather_draws(`cats − lecture`, `puppies − lecture`, `puppies − cats`) %>% 
  mean_qi()
# A tibble: 3 × 7
  .variable         .value .lower .upper .width .point .interval
  <chr>              <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl> <chr>  <chr>    
1 cats − lecture     1.13   0.446   1.80   0.95 mean   qi       
2 puppies − cats     0.445 -0.211   1.10   0.95 mean   qi       
3 puppies − lecture  1.58   0.908   2.23   0.95 mean   qi

Both kinds of animal video clearly beat the stats lecture. Puppies vs. cats? Probably puppies, but we can’t be sure: that interval includes 0. (In the simulation, the true differences are 1.5, 1.9 and 0.4.)

Pairwise differences with marginaleffects

The same comparisons with marginaleffects (each row is a pairwise difference, summarized from the draws):

avg_predictions(a.1, by = "video", hypothesis = ~ pairwise)

            Hypothesis Estimate  2.5 % 97.5 %
 (cats) - (lecture)       1.141  0.446   1.80
 (puppies) - (lecture)    1.582  0.908   2.23
 (puppies) - (cats)       0.448 -0.211   1.10

Type: response

Effect sizes, draw by draw

Code 
post.a.1 %>% 
  gather_draws(`d: cats − lecture`, `d: puppies − lecture`, `d: puppies − cats`) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(y = .variable, x = .value)) +
  stat_halfeye() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = 2) +
  labs(x = "standardized difference (difference / σ)", y = NULL)

Each difference divided by σ, draw by draw, so the effect size gets its own posterior and interval.

Multiple comparison corrections?

Three groups, three pairwise differences. Do we need to correct?

  • On the one hand, multiple comparisons are about error rates, which reference NHST and dichotomous decisions, and we don’t have a null distribution in Bayes land

  • On the other hand, the idea that chance results come up with more shakes of the dice is about probability. We still want to make good decisions and strengthen inferences. Often decisions are needed.

  • With better priors “error rates” decrease. With less dichotomous thinking, error rates also vanish.

  • Bayes solution is better modeling + changing decision criteria

Contrasts with avg_slopes()

For a categorical predictor, avg_slopes() gives each group’s contrast with the reference group (here, the lecture):

library(marginaleffects)
avg_slopes(a.1)

          Contrast Estimate 2.5 % 97.5 %
 cats - lecture        1.14 0.446   1.80
 puppies - lecture     1.58 0.908   2.23

Term: video
Type: response

With more predictors (e.g., group × a continuous variable) this is where marginaleffects really shines; we’ll pick that up in the next lecture on interactions.
